analysis.one_liner: Shortens the monopoly period for brand-name biologic drugs from 12 years to 7.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut biologic drug exclusivity from 12 years to 7 had no cosponsors and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name biologic drugs (advanced medicines made from living cells, like many cancer and arthritis treatments) get 12 years of protection from cheaper copycat versions, called biosimilars. This bill would have cut that monopoly window to 7 years for drugs approved after its enactment, letting competition bring prices down sooner. It was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and never advanced past its first committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take biologics and pay premiums or out-of-pocket costs tied to drug prices would benefit, because biosimilars typically sell at a discount to the brand-name original once allowed on the market. Payers such as employers and government health programs would also see lower drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Public Health Service Act to strike the 12-year marketing exclusivity period for brand-name biological products and replace it with 7 years, allowing biosimilar competitors onto the market five years sooner.

The shortened exclusivity applies only to biological products licensed by the FDA on or after the bill's enactment, so it would not disrupt existing patents but would lower future drug prices over time.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic drugmakers, especially large biopharmaceutical companies that rely on the 12-year exclusivity window to earn premium prices before cheaper biosimilars arrive, would lose five years of monopoly revenue on future products.

drawbacks.text: Biologics are unusually expensive and risky to develop; the 12-year exclusivity window was designed to give companies time to recoup those investments. Cutting it to 7 years could reduce the reward for developing new biologics, and industry groups have long argued this would mean fewer future medicines (this objection is general knowledge about how biologic exclusivity works, not stated in the bill's sources).

The bill only applies to products licensed after enactment, so its benefits are delayed: current blockbuster drugs keep their full exclusivity, and patients would see savings only on future approvals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who need biologics, faster competition is a real gain, since biosimilars reliably undercut brand prices. The tradeoff is a five-year-shorter reward for biologic innovation, a cost that would fall on future patients only if it meaningfully slows new drug development — a contested point the bill's record does not settle. On balance the bill trades some industry revenue for lower prices with a modest lag.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's health subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no committee action.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the PRICED Act in the House on July 26, 2018.
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Health.
No other action was taken; the bill received no cosponsors and the Congress ended January 3, 2019, without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic drugmakers keep the full 12-year exclusivity window, and the five extra years of monopoly pricing on future products are preserved because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, her sole sponsorship of the measure in the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew opposition on the record: it had zero cosponsors, no votes, and no recorded floor or committee debate, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would cut their monopoly window from 12 years to 7 on future products, ending five years of premium pricing before biosimilar competition. Industry has historically defended the 12-year standard as necessary to fund development of expensive-to-make biologics.
Five extra years of open market entry for copycat versions of future biologics would expand the products they can sell. Their gains come from the same price cuts that benefit patients.
